query: For Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 initially in a high-temperature BCC state, the factors governing its phase stability during cooling and subsequent thermal exposure are not understood well enough to account for the range of phases that may appear. What single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain this behavior and why? Define a controlled comparison and baseline, predicted observations relative to that baseline, the conditions under which the hypothesis should and should not apply, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification result.

generation.hypothesis: In Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7, the initially high‐temperature BCC supersaturated solid solution becomes unstable upon moderate cooling because of differential element diffusivities and atomic size mismatches. These induce local segregation and buildup of elastic stresses that, once a critical level is reached, trigger nucleation of secondary ordered phases (e.g., ordered B2 or sigma) at preferential sites such as grain boundaries or dendrite peripheries through mechanisms that include sluggish diffusion typical of multi‐principal element systems.
generation.material_initial_state: Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 in a high-temperature, single-phase BCC (supersaturated) state.
generation.intervention: Subject the alloy to controlled cooling protocols (e.g., rapid quench versus slow cooling) and subsequent isothermal annealing at intermediate temperatures.
generation.conditions: The hypothesis is proposed under conditions where atomic mobility permits elemental partitioning—namely, during slow cooling or moderate annealing—while it should not apply under rapid quenching conditions that freeze in the high-temperature state or at very low temperatures where diffusion is negligible.
generation.structural_mediator: Local elemental segregation that induces lattice distortion and elastic stress fields.
generation.mechanism: Differential diffusivities and atomic size differences promote chemical inhomogeneity during cooling. The resulting segregation creates localized elastic stresses and lattice distortions that lower the energy barrier for nucleating secondary phases (such as ordered B2 or intermetallic sigma phases) at microstructural features like grain boundaries, consistent with sluggish diffusion in multi-principal element systems.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to a rapidly quenched control that retains a single-phase BCC structure, samples cooled slowly and/or annealed at 600–900 °C will show increased elemental segregation, measurable lattice strains, and the nucleation of secondary phases (identified by changes in diffraction patterns and increased microhardness due to interphase boundaries).
generation.baseline: A rapidly quenched Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 sample that maintains a largely uniform BCC phase with minimal elemental segregation and lower internal elastic stresses.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is expected when diffusion rates are sufficient to permit segregation (i.e., at moderate temperatures and cooling rates). It may not hold if kinetic effects completely suppress diffusion (very rapid quenching) or if the alloy composition is altered so that atomic size mismatches and mixing enthalpy differences are minimized.
generation.uncertainty: The precise types of secondary phases (e.g., distinguishing between B2 and sigma) and the quantitative thresholds of elastic stress required for nucleation remain to be fully established.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 specimens: one group is rapidly quenched from the high-temperature BCC state to suppress diffusion, while the other is slowly cooled and subsequently annealed at controlled temperatures (600 °C and 900 °C). Using X-ray diffraction (XRD), scanning electron microscopy (SEM), energy dispersive spectroscopy (EDS), and microhardness testing, compare the phase constitution, elemental segregation, and internal stresses between groups.
measurements: XRD peak splitting or emergence of additional peaks indicating secondary phases
EDS mapping to detect compositional segregation
Microhardness variations correlating with phase transformations
Measurement of lattice strain via high-resolution TEM or XRD line-broadening analysis
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If slow cooling and/or annealing do not result in statistically significant elemental segregation, observable lattice strain, or the nucleation of secondary phases (with corresponding changes in microhardness) relative to the rapidly quenched control, then the proposed stress-driven segregation mechanism is not supported.

cited_evidence.text: A detailed microstructural evaluation was executed on the crystallographic texture as well as the mechanisms for nucleation, phase transformation, and grain growth in a Al0.7CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy. The microstructure and crystallographic orientations were characterized by electron backscatter diffraction, and the chemical composition variations by energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy. The cast Al0.7CoCrFeNi alloy started in the BCC phase and partially transformed into the FCC phase. It was found that the Pitsch orientation relationship (OR) dominates the nucleation mechanism of the FCC phase; however, deviations with respect to the Pitsch OR are observed and are attributed to the differently sized atoms forming an ordered B2 phase in the alloy causing lattice distortions. The dual phase BCC–FCC microstructure contains FCC Widmanstätten plates oriented parallel to the {110}BCC planes of the parent grain. It was found that the crystal orientation distribution after the BCC–FCC phase transformation is confined and is explained as a product of the governing mechanisms.

AbstractIn the present study, powder of FeCoCrNiMo0.5Al1.3 HEA was manufactured by gas atomization process, and then used for laser powder bed fusion (L-PBF) and microplasma spraying (MPS) technologies. The processes of phase composition and microstructure transformation during above mentioned processes and subsequent heat treatment were analyzed by X-ray diffraction (XRD), scanning electron microscopy (SEM), energy dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS), and differential thermal analysis (DTA) methods. It was found that gas atomization leads to a formation of dendrites of body centered cubic (BCC) supersaturated solid solution with insignificant Mo-rich segregations on the peripheries of the dendrites. Annealing leads to an increase of element segregations till to decomposition of the BCC solid solution and formation of σ-phase and B2 phase. Microstructure and phase composition of L-PBF sample are very similar to those of the powder. The MPS coating has a little fraction of face centered cubic (FCC) phase because of Al oxidation during spraying and formation of regions depleted in Al, in which FCC structure becomes more stable.
